sentenceSets.sentence: She attempted to resurrect a proposal that had been tabled two years earlier, arguing that the conditions that had defeated it had changed.

answerChoices.reasoning: Reviving fits something that has weakened and needs strengthening, but this proposal was fully stopped two years ago and has to be brought back from nothing.
Amending changes a proposal's text, whereas her argument is that circumstances rather than the proposal itself have changed.
Revisiting means looking at something again for discussion, while she is trying to put a dead measure back into active play.
Salvaging rescues usable parts from a failure, but she is pressing for the whole proposal on the ground that it would now succeed.
Tabling is exactly what was done to the proposal two years earlier, so doing it again would repeat the setback rather than reverse it.
Circulating merely distributes a document and would not address the defeat the sentence says she is trying to overcome.
Summarizing condenses the proposal and does nothing about its having been defeated.
Endorsing is lending support to something already under consideration, but this proposal has been off the agenda for two years.
Burying the proposal would keep it dead, the opposite of what her argument about changed conditions is meant to accomplish.
Withdrawing removes something from consideration, and the proposal has already been out of consideration for two years.
Ratifying formally approves a measure, a final step that cannot apply to a proposal that is not even before the body.

sentenceSets.sentence: A young conductor has resurrected the symphony, which had not been performed since its disastrous premiere in 1911.

answerChoices.reasoning: Rehabilitating restores a damaged reputation, but the sentence's point is that the music had gone entirely unplayed for over a century, not that it was thought badly of.
Transcribing rewrites a work for different forces, and nothing here suggests the score was altered, only that it was heard again.
Premiering means giving a first performance, which the sentence explicitly assigns to 1911.
Championing means advocating for something over time, while the sentence's contrast with a century of silence points to the act of bringing the piece back into performance.
Recording captures a performance on tape, a narrower act than ending the work's absence from the concert hall.
Composing would make the conductor the author, contradicting the symphony's existence since 1911.
Abridging shortens a work, which says nothing about why it had gone unperformed for so long.
Cataloguing records the work in a list, an archival act that would not bring it back to the stage.
Suppressing the symphony would keep it silent, extending rather than ending the century of neglect.
Shelving puts a work away, the opposite of the conductor's achievement described here.
Auctioning sells an object, and a symphony's return to performance is not a sale.

sentenceSets.sentence: Every few years a tabloid resurrects the old rumor about the actress, and every few years her lawyers kill it again.

answerChoices.reasoning: Recycling implies reusing material that has stayed in circulation, but the lawyers kill the rumor each time, so it must be brought back from the dead rather than simply reused.
Embellishing adds invented detail to a story already in play, whereas this rumor has been extinguished before each reappearance.
Corroborating supplies supporting evidence, which is hard to square with a story her lawyers are able to shut down every time.
Retracting withdraws a published claim, which is what the lawyers force rather than what the tabloid does every few years.
Denying the rumor would put the tabloid on the actress's side, contradicting the fight her lawyers must repeatedly win.
Investigating is sober inquiry, while the sentence describes a cycle of publication and legal suppression rather than research.
Licensing is a matter of paying for rights to content, which has nothing to do with a rumor being killed by lawyers.
Ignoring the rumor would give her lawyers nothing to kill every few years.
Burying the rumor is what the lawyers accomplish, the opposite of what the tabloid keeps doing.
Praising a rumor makes no sense as a description of tabloid behavior that provokes legal action.
Translating moves text between languages and has no connection to a rumor's repeated revival.
